title: SRE standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, and runbooks
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for service level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning methodology, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and a canonical runbook structure. It is intended for SREs, on-call engineers, service owners, and engineering managers. Follow these standards to ensure consistent measurement, blameless postmortems, predictable capacity, and reliable automatic and manual mitigations.

Goals
- Define a consistent SLO and error-budget lifecycle for all public-facing and internal services.
- Standardize capacity planning inputs and forecasting cadence.
- Provide clear templates and expectations for incident reviews and runbooks.
- Maintain a small set of curated operational tools and dashboards for on-call efficiency.

Scope
Includes Redwood-hosted control plane services, inference runtime services (request-router, runtime-pool, cache-layer, model-store), and critical infra (auth, metrics, alerting). Excludes ephemeral developer tooling unless it impacts customer-visible SLOs.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Key concepts (definitions)
- SLI (Service Level Indicator): Measurable signal reflecting user experience (e.g., p50 request latency for /v1/generate, successful inference responses).
- SLO: Target for an SLI over a defined window (e.g., 99.9% uptime over a 30d window).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO; the allowable fraction of bad requests during the window.
- Burn rate: Speed at which the error budget is consumed.

SLO lifecycle and ownership
- Every customer-facing service must have an owner and a documented SLO. Service owners are responsible for defining SLIs, SLO targets, and error budget policies.
- SRE team reviews new SLOs during design/launch and annually during reliability planning.
- SLO documents must include measurement: metric source (Prometheus/OTEL), aggregation method, and alerting thresholds.

Standard SLO tiers (recommended)
- Critical (APIs serving production inference): Availability 99.95% (30d), Latency p95 & p99 targets per route.
- High (supporting infra like model-store read): Availability 99.9% (30d).
- Standard (internal batch jobs): Availability 99.0% (30d).

SLO table (examples)
| Service | SLI | SLO (30d) | Measurement | Alert threshold | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| Request-router (public API) | Successful user-response rate | 99.95% | prom/routing_success_rate (30d) | 99.90% (alert) | eng-sre/request-router |
| Runtime-pool (inference) | p95 response latency (ms) | p95 <= 350ms | prom/runtime_p95 | p95 > 450ms (alert) | eng-serving-runtime |
| Model-store | Object read success | 99.9% | prom/modelstore_reads_success | 99.5% | eng-platform |

Error budget policy (standard)
- When burn rate > 2x for 1h: paging to on-call SRE and notify service owner.
- When burn rate > 4x for 30m: require incident review within 24h and freeze risky changes (deploy hold) to the service.
- When error budget is fully exhausted: automatic rollback to last known good can be triggered for high-risk changes; otherwise, deployment freeze enforced until budget recovery.

Alerting and escalation
- Alerts map to a three-tier system: Actionable (page SRE oncall), Attention (Slack channel + email), Informational (dashboard-only).
- Every paging alert must include: impact statement, start time, current burn rate, and recommended first actions.

2) Capacity planning

Principles
- Plan for 99th-percentile peak workload with headroom for bursty traffic: target 25-40% headroom on production clusters for inference pools based on model mix.
- Use telemetry and load tests (benchmark suite) to estimate per-model GPU/CPU consumption and concurrency.
- Short-term scaling: autoscaling and pre-warming. Long-term: reserved capacity purchases and cluster growth planning.

Inputs and cadence
- Inputs: rolling 90d usage, per-customer usage trends, new product launches, upcoming model onboarding, quantization/optimization changes.
- Cadence: weekly 1w lookahead for autoscaling configs; monthly capacity review for infra commits; quarterly forecasting for reserved capacity (Dedicated).

Capacity model (summary table)
| Dimension | Data source | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| GPU pool utilization | Prometheus + telemetry | eng-infra/gpu-fleet |
| Per-model token/sec cost | Benchmark suite (bench/perf) | eng-serving-runtime |
| Customer committed throughput | Billing/usage DB | finance + sales |

Headroom policy and scaling actions
- Soft target: keep trailing 24h utilization below 75% on critical pools.
- If projected utilization > 80% in next 7d: trigger capacity runbook (see Runbooks section) and notify capacity_planning@redwood.com.
- Autoscaler config should prefer adding nodes (scale out) before increasing per-node concurrency.

3) Reliability initiatives and SLO-driven work

Prioritization
- Reliability initiatives are prioritized based on SLO impact, error-budget burn, customer impact, and cost. Use a simple scoring rubric: SLO impact (1-5), customer-critical (1-5), effort estimate (T-shirt).

Examples of recurring initiatives
- Prefix/KV cache efficiency improvements to reduce p95 latency by 20%.
- Kernel/kernel-selection improvements to cut per-token cost on T4/RTX fleets.
- End-to-end synthetic tests for critical routes to catch regressions pre-deploy.

Ownership and roadmap alignment
- Each initiative has: owner, target SLO delta, rollout plan (canary -> ramp -> full), rollback criteria. Track initiatives in eng-platform roadmap under the "reliability" theme.

4) Incident review standards (postmortems)

Objectives
- Capture timeline and impact, root cause analysis, contributing factors, corrective actions, and follow-up tasks with owners and due dates.
- Emphasize blameless investigations and systemic fixes.

Postmortem template (required fields)
1) Incident summary (one-paragraph)
2) Impact (customer-visible metrics, affected services, duration)
3) Timeline (UTC timestamps, actions taken)
4) Root cause analysis (why and how)
5) Contributing factors (process, tooling, monitoring gaps)
6) Mitigation and recovery steps (what was done to restore service)
7) Follow-up actions (owner, due date, verification criteria)
8) Lessons learned and checklist updates

SLA for reviews
- Sev 1 incidents: publish postmortem within 72h; review in SRE weekly triage within 7 days.
- Sev 2 incidents: publish postmortem within 7 days.

Moderation and distribution
- Postmortems are reviewed by at least one SRE reviewer and the service owner. Summaries are posted to #sre-postmortems and linked in the service's confluence page.

5) Operational tooling and dashboards

Required dashboards (minimum)
- Global SLO dashboard: current SLOs, budgets, burn rates (30d & 1h) across all critical services.
- Per-service runbook dashboard: SLI graphs, alert counts, recent deploys, and golden metrics.
- Capacity dashboard: cluster utilization, per-node GPU memory/compute, pending pods, and scaling events.
- Incident triage board: active incidents, owners, and status.

Tooling stack (approved)
- Metrics & alerting: Prometheus + Cortex (long-term), Alertmanager.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry -> Jaeger/Tempo.
- Logs: Loki / ELK for indexed logs.
- On-call: PagerDuty (paging), Slack (alerts & comms).
- Runbook/Docs: Confluence (this repo) + runbook snippets in GitHub under infra/runbooks.

Automation expectations
- On-call playbooks should be automatable where possible: common mitigations implemented as scripts or runbooks in GitHub Actions / ops-libs.
- Deploy hold and automatic rollback are implemented as pipeline gates for production services when error budget rules are triggered.

6) SRE runbooks (canonical format)

Runbook metadata (top of document)
- Title: short identifier (e.g., request-router-high-error-rate)
- Service: request-router
- Owner: eng-sre/request-router
- Pager: @sre-oncall (PagerDuty link)
- Last tested: YYYY-MM-DD

Runbook sections (standard)
1) Symptom and impact: What to expect, indicators and dashboards to check.
2) Safe first actions (fastest lowest-risk mitigations).
3) Triage checklist (commands, queries to run).
4) Mitigation steps (ordered, with rollbacks).
5) Communication templates (Slack + status page blurb).
6) Recovery verification and post-incident tasks.

Example: request-router - high 5xx rate
- Symptom: sudden increase in 5xx rate for /v1/generate; SLO burn rate > 3x; users report errors.
- Safe first actions:
  1) Check global SLO dashboard and request-router dashboard.
  2) Verify recent deploys: curl the service-control API to list vhosts and active binary: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://control-plane.internal/v1/deploys?service=request-router
  3) If a deploy is recent (<30m) and coincides with spike, consider immediate rollback to previous deploy (see rollback checklist).
- Triage commands (examples):
  - promql: increase(prometheus_request_errors_total[5m]) / increase(prometheus_request_total[5m])
  - kubectl: kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=request-router -o wide
  - logs: loki query: {app="request-router"} |~ "ERROR" | line_format "{{.message}}"
- Mitigation steps:
  1) If pod OOMs or crashloops observed: scale down concurrency and place a temporary autoscale cap.
  2) If service-wide regression after deploy: execute controlled rollback via CI; include smoke test verification.
  3) If backend dependency (model-store) degraded: switch runtime to degraded-mode pool (lower quality but stable).
- Communication templates:
  - Slack status: "[INCIDENT] request-router 5xx spike. Impact: public inference failures. Oncall: @sre-oncall. Initial mitigation: rollback in progress."
  - Status page blurb: "We are investigating increased error rates for inference requests. Some customers may experience failures. Updates every 15 minutes."
- Recovery verification:
  - Confirm SLO metrics returning to baseline and burn rate dropping below 1.5x for 1h.
  - Run a canary test with representative prompts across top-5 models.

Runbook maintenance and testing
- Runbooks must be reviewed every 6 months and after each incident where they were used. Record "Last tested" and test results (pass/fail summary) in the runbook header.
- On-call game-days: quarterly exercises to validate runbooks and automation.

Appendix A: Alerts and thresholds (common)
- request-router-5xx-high: page when 5xx rate > 0.5% for 5m OR burst error-budget burn rate > 2x.
- runtime-p95-slo-breach: page when p95 > 450ms for 10m.
- modelstore-read-failure: attention when read-failure rate > 0.5% for 15m.

Appendix B: Post-incident action checklist (must be assigned)
1) Create postmortem draft within SLA.
2) Assign follow-ups with owners and due dates.
3) Add checklist changes to runbooks and playbooks.
4) Schedule a retro if repeat incident pattern detected.
